title: Why You'd Never Want To Swim With A Saltwater Crocodile

scenes.notes: If you're swimming off northern Australia and the water looks completely empty, that's when you should worry.
The saltwater crocodile is the biggest reptile alive. Big males pass six metres and weigh a full tonne.
And it goes out to sea. Tagged crocs have ridden ocean currents for hundreds of kilometres between islands.

scenes.notes: It can rest underwater for over an hour. Only its eyes and nostrils need to break the surface.
When it strikes, it closes with the strongest bite ever measured in a living animal. Strong enough to crack a sea turtle's shell.
Then it drags you under and spins, until you can't tell which way is up.
So, your options. Swim for the shore? In the water, it's faster than you will ever be.
Run zigzag on land? That one's a myth. Just run straight. Crocs rarely chase you far from the water.
Play dead? It was going to drag you under anyway.
The only option that works is the boring one. Stay away from the water's edge. That's where nearly every attack begins.
Here's what surprises people. The croc you can see isn't the problem. It's the one that has watched you for days, and learned exactly when you come down to the water.

scenes.notes: So next time the water looks empty, remember. Empty is what it looks like when a crocodile is doing its job. Ever swum somewhere with croc signs? Tell me where.
